items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the limited liability company law, the tax law, the
administrative code of the city of New York, and the executive law, in
relation to the disclosure of beneficial owners of limited liability companies
and certain other business entities
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8439

SPONSOR: HOYLMAN
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the limited liability company law, the tax law, the
administrative code of the city of New York, and the executive law, in
relation to the disclosure of beneficial owners of limited liability
companies and certain other business entities

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill aims to provide full transparency for the beneficial owners of
limited liability companies in New York by defining beneficial owner-
ship, requiring annual disclosure on tax returns, and publishing benefi-
cial owners of limited liability companies in New York's publicly
searchable corporation and business entity database.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

  Section  one  amends the limited liability company (LLC) law to define
beneficial ownership, i.e. the individual  people  who  actually  profit
from  or  control  a  corporation  or  asset. Provisions are included to
ensure that certain parties, such as creditors, minors, or employees  of
worker  cooperatives (among others) are not included for the purposes of
the law. Since corporate  entities  can  also  be  members  of  an  LLC,
provisions are included for disclosing the beneficial owners or officers
of other corporate entities that may comprise an LLC's membership.

  Section  two  amends  the LLC law to require that a list of beneficial
owners of an LLC be included with the documents necessary to organize an
LLC in New York State. The information provided  must  include  a  name,
current  business  address,  and a number from a non-expired passport or
driver's license.

  Section three permits the Department  of  State  to  check  for  legal
sufficiency  the list of beneficial owners included with an LLC's organ-
ization documents.

  Section four amends the LLC law to  create  a  new  section,  215,  to
require  the Department of State to preserve beneficial ownership infor-
mation for any LLC for a period of five years after an LLC has ceased to
exist and also provides penalties for the willful  filing  of  false  or
fraudulent beneficial ownership information.

  Section  five  amends the tax law to permit the Department of Taxation
and Finance to  share  beneficial  ownership  information  disclosed  on
returns by LLC filers with the Department of State.

  Section  six  amends  the LLC law to require that a list of beneficial
owners of an LLC be included with the documents necessary to register an
out-of-state LLC to do business  in  New  York  State.  The  information
provided  must  include  a  name, current business address, and a number
from a non-expired passport or driver's license.

  Section seven amends the LLC law to create  a  new  section,  810,  to
require  the Department of State to preserve beneficial ownership infor-
mation for any out-of-state LLC registered to do business  in  New  York
for  a  period of five years after an LLC has ceased to be registered in
New York and also provides penalties for the willful filing of false  or
fraudulent beneficial ownership information.

  Section  eight amends the tax law to require the disclosure of benefi-
cial owners of LLCs acquiring residential real property on deed transfer
forms filed with the Department of Taxation and Finance.  Previously the
law required the disclosure of members and  managers  of  LLCs  on  such
forms  but  only  applying to residential real property with one to four
units.

  Section nine amends the New York City Administrative Code  to  require
the  same  disclosure of beneficial ownership information on residential
real property deed transfer forms in New York City.

  Section ten amends the tax law to require the Department  of  Taxation
and  Finance  to release to the Department of State beneficial ownership
information gained through tax returns or any other means.

  Section eleven requires that the  Department  of  State  assign  every
beneficial  owner of an LLC a unique identifying number and publish such
number in relation to any affiliated LLCs in the Department  of  State's
corporation  and business entity database, which is publicly searchable.
The names and business of any beneficial owner shall be  accessible  via
FOIL, although they shall not be published in the corporation and entity
database  for  privacy  reasons.  A  waiver process for individuals with
significant privacy interests is created to prevent  the  disclosure  of
those  individuals'  names  and  businesses addresses via FOIL, although
their unique identifying number may remain in the corporation and  busi-
ness  entity  database.  The  Department  of State is also authorized to
verify beneficial ownership information in the database with information
submitted by the Department of Taxation and Finance and may,  if  incon-
sistencies  in  beneficial  ownership  information indicate fraud, refer
such suspected fraud to the relevant authorities.

  Section twelve amends the tax law to require that LLCs include benefi-
cial ownership information in their annual tax returns and that an annu-
al tax return shall not be accepted without the inclusion of such infor-
mation. The Department of Taxation and Finance is further authorized  to
verify beneficial ownership information included in LLC tax returns with
beneficial  ownership  information submitted to the Department of State,
and if inconsistencies are revealed that  indicate  potential  fraud  or
suspicious  activity,  to refer such suspicions to the relevant authori-
ties.

  Section thirteen is the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Anonymous corporate ownership has proliferated since the 1990s  and  has
created  numerous public policy problems locally, nationally, and inter-
nationally. In 2015, the New York Times published a series  of  investi-
gative reports called "Towers of Secrecy" that revealed that many condo-
miniums in a Manhattan skyscraper were owned by high-profile individuals
under investigation or sanctions for crimes such as money-laundering and
embezzlement.  LLC  laws have enabled these individuals, whose purchases
may have otherwise  been  scrutinized  by  international  legal  or  tax
authorities,  to purchase assets in New York through anonymous and prac-
tically untraceable shell corporations. In 2019, a  local  newspaper  in
Cleveland broke the news that the largest commercial real estate holders
in  Cleveland were two Ukrainian oligarchs who purchased extensive prop-
erties throughout  the  downtown  business  district  with  hundreds  of
millions  of  dollars  laundered  through shell corporations. And a 2019
report commissioned by the New York Senate Committee  on  Investigations
and  Government  Operations found that opaque LLC ownership had hampered
code inspectors and code enforcement in upstate communities for years. A
Pew Stateline story in 2019 reported that this problem  was  nationwide,
prompting both Arizona and Washington to enact legislation that required
LLC  ownership  information  to  be registered in a state database. More
recently, tenants have been unable to receive  funds  disbursed  through
the  Emergency Rental Assistance Program because anonymous LLC landlords
have not completed their half of the application and have been unreacha-
ble by tenants or state authorities. Pointing to a sociological explana-
tion for neglect in deteriorating housing markets, a paper in the Ameri-
can Sociological Review in 2019 described an  "LLC  effect"  responsible
for  negligent  property  ownership  behavior.  Analyzing  thousands  of
records from Milwaukee's rental market and controlling for all  possible
confounding  variables,  the  author  found  that  LLC's  anonymity  and
protections against liability  facilitate  negligent  behavior,  because
property  owners  do not need to be publicly identified as slumlords and
liability protections reduce risks for landlords  who  forego  necessary
maintenance  or  violate  building  standards.  These  forces combine to
create hazards for municipal governments  seeking  to  enforce  building
codes and tenants forced to live in substandard conditions.

Leaks  such  as  the  Panama  Papers  and  the  Pandora Papers have also
revealed the extent  of  which  money  is  laundered  globally  for  the
purposes  of  tax avoidance through anonymous shell corporations such as
LLCs. In 2013, the G8 nations adopted a statement of principles relating
to  the  disclosure  of  beneficial  ownership  information,  which  was
expanded and adopted by the G20 in 2014 after the release of guidance by
the international Financial Action Task Force. In 2016, the United King-
dom  committed  to creating three public registries of beneficial owner-
ship information for real property, corporations, and trusts. In Europe,
the European Union directed member states to create publicly  searchable
registries of beneficial ownership information for corporate entities by
January  2020  and  another for trusts and similar legal arrangements by
March 2020. These registries were required to be connected to a  central
platform  by  March 10, 2021. In the United States, the National Defense
Authorization Act for 2021 authorized the Treasury Department  to  begin
collecting beneficial ownership information in a database called FinCEN,
so requiring these disclosures in New York should not be burdensome.

This  bill  builds  on previous efforts to require the disclosure of LLC
members and managers involved in real estate transactions in  New  York.
The  bill  extends  disclosure requirements to all LLCs registered to do
business in New York. By placing beneficial ownership information  in  a
public  database, government and public policy researchers can study who
actually owns what in New York, a task that has become  impossible  with
the  proliferation of anonymous LLCs in the real estate market beginning
in the 1990s. The database would also help eliminate the possibility  of
money-laundering  or tax avoidance through anonymous shell corporations,
and residential and commercial tenants will also  benefit  from  knowing
who their landlord actually is.

The  LLC  was  only  invented  in 1977 by the Wyoming state legislature,
blessed by the IRS in 1988, and adopted as a form of corporate organiza-
tion in New York in 1994. The anonymity of ownership of LLCs  and  other
shell corporations has helped create numerous public policy problems and
this bill will help fix them.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

This is a new bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This  bill  is  effective  365 days after becoming law, provided however
that the repeal, amendment, or  enactment  of  any  rule  or  regulation
necessary to effectuate the meaning or purpose of this law on its effec-
tive  date  is  authorized  to be made or completed before its effective
date.

A.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the limited liability company law, in relation to the
disclosure of beneficial owners of limited liability companies
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8439A

SPONSOR: HOYLMAN
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the limited liability company law, in relation to the
disclosure of beneficial owners of limited liability companies

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill aims to modernize disclosure laws for limited liability compa-
nies by defining beneficial ownership and requiring the disclosure of
beneficial owners.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section one is the short title.

Section two amends the LLC law to define beneficial ownership, exclude
certain individuals from qualifying as beneficial owners, and capture
indirect forms of beneficial ownership, including through trusts and
intermediaries.

Section three amends the LLC law to require that a document identifying
the beneficial owners of an LLC be included with the documents necessary
to organize an LLC in New York State.

Section four amends the LLC law to require an amendment to the documents
necessary to organize an LLC in New York State if there is a change to
the beneficial owners of the LLC.

Section five amends the LLC law to create a new section requiring the
disclosure of beneficial ownership and permits the LLC to file a copy of
the same form they file with the federal government.

Section six amends the LLC law to require that a document identifying
the beneficial owners of an LLC be included with the documents necessary
to organize a foreign LLC in New York State.

Section seven amends the LLC law, pertaining to foreign LLCS, to require
an amendment to the documents necessary to organize a foreign LLC in New
York State if there is a change to the beneficial owners of the foreign
LLC.

Section eight amends the LLC law, pertaining to foreign LLCS, to create
a new section requiring the disclosure of beneficial ownership and
permits the foreign LLC to file a copy of the same form they file with
the federal government.

Section nine is the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Anonymous shell companies have been exploited as vehicles for money
laundering, tax evasion, organized crime, terrorist financing, and other
forms of corruption for decades. In the United States, the most common
form of a shell corporation is the limited liability company ("LLC"). To
form an LLC, a person needs less personal information than is required
to obtain a library card. The true owners of LLCs can be concealed even
further through trusts and nesting layers of corporate intermediaries,
facilitating money laundering, crime, and tax avoidance as assets become
washed through anonymous legal entities. Billions of dollars from the
illicit gains of international kleptocrats have been washed through LLCs
in the United States, becoming nearly impossible to trace without
tremendous effort. These phenomena have been thoroughly documented by
leaks and investigations such as the Panama Papers in 2016 and Pandora
Papers in 2021.

Anonymous LLCs have also been vehicles for narcotics and human traffick-
ers to launder their illicit profits and escape accountability. The
sociologist Adam Travis has documented an "LLC effect" in housing
markets, which is a statistically significant correlation between code
violations and the prevalence of LLC landlords caused by the combination
of anonymity and limited liability protections. This effect was demon-
strated by a 2019 Senate investigation into housing code violations in
the Hudson Valley.  Anonymous LLCs have also continued to facilitate
campaign finance violations despite recent legislation prohibiting this
practice.

Beneficial ownership transparency, which includes disclosure and public
reporting, is the internationally-recognized gold standard for combating
these forms of crime and corruption. This bill would make New York a
national leader in terms of addressing the public policy problems
created by anonymous shell corporations. This legislation would be a
significant deterrent to corruption, fraud, and organized crime. It
would ease the investigative burden on law enforcement authorities pros-
ecuting financial crimes and the regulatory burden imposed on businesses
required to report the beneficial owners of their customers pursuant to
federal law, such as title agencies and financial institutions. Tenants
would be able to know who their landlord is, researchers and policy-mak-
ers would be better able to understand business and investment patterns
otherwise made opaque by LLCs, and the government would be able to veri-
fy the beneficial owners of LLCs involved in procurement processes.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

This is a new bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This bill is effective 365 days after becoming law, provided however
that the repeal, amendment, or enactment of any rule or regulation
necessary to effectuate the meaning or purpose of this law on its effec-
tive date is authorized to be made or completed before its effective
date.
